item.title: Therapists Ignore AI at Their Own Peril
item.description:
Psych Careers

Therapists Ignore AI at Their Own Peril

Personal Perspective: Facing industry shifts is the only way to remain relevant.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • An APA survey showed almost 38% of the population studied found LLM’s more helpful than traditional therapy.
  • AI outperformed human group therapy in a major RCT. The profession needs to talk about this.
  • Competition brings down prices, and chatbots used for support can be considered our competition.
  • The clinicians most certain AI can't replace us may be the ones who've never really tried it.

I took a continuing education class yesterday in which a colleague assured the audience that AI won't take our jobs. It wasn't the first time I've heard this in a CE setting. And each time it happens, I find myself more stunned than the last.

Source: Image created by ChatGPT

It is time for us, as a profession, to grapple with a rapidly changing future. If we cannot face disruption in our own professional lives, how will we help our clients face it in theirs? We only empower AI when we pretend we aren't competing with it.

AI's Impact on Earnings and Career Sustainability

Let's start with the most common one: You'll keep your job. Maybe. But keeping your job and having your job remain untouched are two entirely different things. As AI therapy advances, it creates genuine market competition. In every market competition drives prices down.

Thus, at minimum, the inevitable impact of AI on our profession will be reduce fees, but also likely the respect our degrees garnish when we are competing with an algorithm. Many young clinicians graduate with substantial debt, and this salary reduction changes the economics of entering this field entirely. The argument that therapists won't lose jobs sidesteps a harder question: Whether the jobs that remain will be sustainable or well-compensated. If salaries decline, the cost of training for this profession has to change accordingly. That conversation is not happening.

Will Clients Prefer Human or AI Therapists in the Future?

The second reassurance is equally fragile. The argument is, there are so many untreated people who need mental health care, and so few therapists, that AI will simply expand access rather than replace us. There's some truth here. But this argument has a hidden assumption that deserves examination.

For humans to maintain a meaningful role in the profession, three things have to be true simultaneously. A sufficient number of clients must prefer a human therapist over an AI, must prefer it enough to pay dramatically more for the privilege, and must be willing to tolerate the scheduling challenges that inevitably arise when scheduling with a human. A chatbot provides unlimited and completely flexible therapeutic interaction for roughly twenty dollars a month. A human therapist costs anywhere from one hundred fifty to three hundred dollars an hour and has scheduling limits such as limited evening and weekend time. Even people who genuinely prefer human connection have to prefer it at an extraordinary price and conveniance differential. That bar will get higher as AI improves.

And consider this: a 2025 APA peer-reviewed study by Rousmaniere and colleagues surveyed nearly 500 Americans with ongoing mental health conditions who had used AI in the past year. When comparing LLM’s to human therapy, almost 38% found LLM’s more helpful than traditional therapy. While only one study, it nonetheless deserves attention.

Key Findings Comparing AI and Human Therapy

The research is moving faster than the profession wants to acknowledge. Just months ago, a randomized controlled trial published in JAMA Network Open compared AI therapy, face-to-face group therapy, and a waitlist control in nearly a thousand college students. AI outperformed group therapy on anxiety and beat both groups on well-being and life satisfaction.

Again, one study proves nothing. But here's what the profession keeps missing: this is a moment in time. AI is improving at a pace humans can’t. The question is not whether today's chatbots match the best human therapists. The question is where the trajectory leads. And the trajectory is not ambiguous to me. Like the vast majority of occupations, chatbots will transform our profession and challenge our livelihoods.

How Important Is Perceived Therapeutic Alliance?

Then there is the therapeutic alliance argument. The relationship is what heals, the thinking goes, and AI cannot form a real relationship. Yet people anthropomorphize AI and report feeling genuinely connected to chatbots. The JAMA study found that perceived therapeutic alliance with the AI platform predicted engagement, which predicted symptom improvement. Furthermore, a substantial number of people actively prefer AI for mental health support precisely because it isn’t human. For clients feeling shame or who are fearful of judgement, a kind and gentle algorhythm can feel more soothing than a person.

There is also a disruption that we aren’t tracking at all: What chatbots do best right now is help the “worried well.” This is the same population newly minted-therapists learn on. Assuming many opt for nearly free AI care, our youngest professionals will lose their training ground. Clinical expertise is built incrementally. A profession where the lower end of the acuity spectrum disappears will struggle to develop the next generation of competent specialists. Again, nobody is talking about this.

Cost-Effectiveness May Be the Bottom Line

Insurers are watching all of this. Whether human therapists remain economically viable in a landscape where AI demonstrates comparable outcomes for common presentations is not a question payers will answer sentimentally. They will follow cost-effectiveness data. And we may already be seeing the first signs. Recently, one major insurer quietly reduced reimbursement rates for doctoral-level therapists to the level of master's-prepared clinicians, effectively erasing the financial return on years of additional training. Most therapists I've spoken with had no idea this happened. That's a problem. By the time these shifts become impossible to ignore, the window for responding will have narrowed considerably. If you still question this logic, I’m guessing you haven’t actually used a chatbot to work through something that genuinely matters to you. Whenever I do so, I’m shocked by how heard and seen I can feel.

Nonetheless, the problems with AI therapy are real and serious. Chatbots are sycophantic by design, telling users what feels good rather than what is true. They make things up, and they do it confidently, without any signal that something has gone wrong. They work outside the ethical and legal accountability structures that govern licensed practice. And whatever privacy they promise is largely illusory.

We Need to Grapple with AI Disruption Now

I am not at all enthusiastic about the upcoming changes to our profession, nor am I suggesting we capitulate and hand our clients over to machines. I am arguing that our denial is not a winning strategy, and we can’t solve a problem that we don’t understand. The therapists who will navigate this well are the ones willing to look at it clearly now, before the transformation occurs.

We encourage our clients to tolerate uncertainty, adapt to change, and face hard truths rather than avoid them. Let’s take our own advice. We know better than anyone that denial is not a coping strategy. The therapists who will thrive in the next decade are not the ones who were reassured in a CE class. They are the ones who see the change coming, ask hard questions, and adapt. That process starts with honesty with each other, and with ourselves. I’m not a professional seer, and it’s possible I could be wrong. But we can all agree that somethings afoot, and I suggest we pay attention.

item.title: Did Consciousness Begin With Hunger and Sexual Desire?
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Did Consciousness Begin With Hunger and Sexual Desire?

Why do hunger and sexual desire feel so powerful?

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Life revolves around energy acquisition and successful reproduction.
  • Hunger translates metabolic needs into conscious behavioral motivation.
  • Sexual desire transforms reproductive priorities into subjective experience.

Everyone knows what hunger feels like. It can dominate attention, shape decisions, and drive behavior. Sexual desire can do the same. Yet we rarely ask why evolution chose to make these biological needs felt rather than merely regulated.

Although life is very complex and remarkably diverse in its forms on Earth, its fundamental principles are surprisingly similar among living beings. Every living organism, from a single cell to a complex animal, must acquire energy and maintain its complex organization long enough to reproduce. Countless adaptations have evolved in living organisms to better meet these two biological demands. Long before the emergence of nervous systems, living cells evolved sophisticated mechanisms to sense nutrient and energy availability and to coordinate these signals with growth and cell division. These processes became tightly integrated, enabling organisms to allocate resources between survival and reproduction based on environmental conditions [1].

With the evolution of nervous systems, these ancient biological priorities acquired a new dimension, allowing organisms, at least in humans, not only to regulate their internal state but also to experience it. Hunger and satiety signaled the status of energy balance, while sexual desire and satisfaction indicated reproductive opportunities and outcomes. These experiences were not merely sensations; they were biologically meaningful states that motivated organisms to act in ways that promoted survival and reproduction.

Single cells regulate nutrients and reproduction without awareness. Yet in organisms with nervous systems, these biological requirements are often accompanied by subjective experiences. Hunger is not merely low energy availability. It feels like something. Sexual desire is not merely hormonal signaling. It feels like something. Perhaps the emergence of consciousness was not an accidental byproduct of complex brains, but an evolutionary innovation that transformed biological necessities into experienced motivations.

Satiety and hunger are subjective experiences for which we know the mechanisms

Hunger and satiety are not merely simple reflexes in humans; rather, they are subjective experiences shaped by the brain to regulate food intake behavior. The feeling of an empty, growling stomach is driven by ghrelin, the primary hunger hormone. Ghrelin activates neurons in the hypothalamus, generating the conscious and often intrusive experience of craving and the urge to seek food.

After eating, a cascade of satiety signals is triggered. The stomach stretches, and gut hormones such as peptide YY and glucagon-like peptide-1 are released. Simultaneously, the pancreas releases insulin in response to rising blood glucose levels, and the long-term hormone leptin informs the brain that energy needs are met. These signals converge on the hypothalamus and brainstem, effectively suppressing hunger circuits. The resulting subjective experience is one of fullness, contentment, and the disappearance of food-related thoughts, the pleasant sensation of "enough" [2].

article continues after advertisement

These conscious experiences help to maintain energy balance, although it can be influenced by stress, environmental cues, and highly palatable foods, all of which can alter both hormonal signaling and the subjective experience of appetite. Moreover, the brain does not simply react to physiological needs. As a predictive organ, it continuously generates expectations about future energy demands based on prior experience and learned eating patterns. Consequently, feelings of hunger may arise in anticipation of habitual mealtimes, even when the body's immediate metabolic requirements are minimal.

Lust and satisfaction: conscious experiences in the service of reproduction

If hunger is the conscious representation of energetic needs, sexual desire is the conscious representation of reproductive priorities. Hunger and satiety provide surviving long enough to reproduce; however, sexual desire and sexual satisfaction are conscious experiences to make sure reproduction.

Sexual desire arises from the integration of hormonal signals, sensory cues, memories, and social context within distributed neural circuits involving the hypothalamus, limbic system, and reward pathways. Hormones such as testosterone, estrogen, oxytocin, and dopamine influence these circuits, modulating both motivation and reward. Importantly, these physiological processes are experienced subjectively as desire, attraction, anticipation, and satisfaction. As with hunger and satiety, conscious sexual experiences transform underlying biological imperatives into psychologically meaningful states that guide behavior toward reproductive goals. The parallel between feeding and reproduction is striking. In both cases, homeostatic or evolutionary demands are translated into subjective experiences that motivate behavior [3].

Reciprocal interplay between satiety/hunger and sexual desire/satisfaction

If basic conscious experiences, such as hunger, fear, anger, sexual arousal, and satisfaction, arise from instincts derived from fundamental aspects of living beings, then we should observe traces of these fundamental characteristics within those complex subjective qualities. Pathways involved in energy acquisition and reproduction interact at the cellular level. Lower cellular energy, resulting from decreased activity in energy production pathways, inhibits cell division, while regulators of cellular proliferation reciprocally influence energy metabolism pathways. But at the level of the mind, does hunger contribute to sexual desire, or does sexual satisfaction affect appetite? Research has shown that fasting and calorie restriction decrease reproductive hormone levels and subsequently reducing sexual desire. Chronic energy deficiency suppresses libido. Low leptin levels or pathological conditions such as anorexia nervosa are often associated with diminished sexual interest. However, these factors do not solely determine sexual behavior, as psychological, cultural, social, and hormonal influences can override metabolic signals in humans.

Overall, these observations raise an intriguing possibility: conscious experiences may represent an evolutionary innovation that transformed biological needs into felt motivations. Hunger and sexual desire may have been the first qualia—the first experiences that felt like something. If so, then every other conscious experience, from the joy of a beautiful sunset to the anguish of injustice, is a later elaboration of these ancient biological signals. Consciousness, in this view, is not a mystery to be solved. It is the voice of life itself, speaking in hungers and desires [4].

item.title: “Modern” Parenting, Broken Kids?
item.description:
Parenting

“Modern” Parenting, Broken Kids?

What ancient parenting can tell us about the childhood mental health epidemic.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Changes in family structure and culture may play a larger role in child mental health than we acknowledge.
  • The rise of mental health conditions might in part be a byproduct of stressed, overworked, isolated families.
  • Nonwestern, more traditional parenting relied on community, contribution, and calm authority.
  • What if the problem isn't inside the child, but changes we've made in the world surrounding them?
Source: Author: AI Generated

We are in the midst of a childhood mental health epidemic, and one thing is clear: Our children are suffering.

The causes of the epidemic are multiple and varied. For example, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt (2024) has argued convincingly that smartphones and social media have taken a toll on children’s well-being.

The Impact of Shifting Parenting Practices Over Time

Another factor, however, deserves attention: the possibility that in less than a century, modern Western families have drifted away from parenting practices that existed for millennia, which likely helped children become more cooperative, emotionally stable, and resilient.

Journalist Michaeleen Doucleff explored this question in her book Hunt, Gather, Parent: What Ancient Cultures Can Teach Us About the Lost Art of Raising Happy, Helpful Little Humans, where she spent time with Maya, Inuit, and Hadzabe families and contrasted their child-rearing practices with modern Western norms (Doucleff, 2021).

This article considers how her core insights may intersect with the mental health epidemic: whether some portion of the epidemic is caused by a mismatch between children’s needs and modern family life.

Doucleff argues that traditional families often rely on a different parenting structure: Children are embedded in a wider network of extended family, older children are expected to contribute to household life, and adults tend to guide with calm, confident authority rather than constant verbal correction or child-centered negotiation. Instead of organizing family life around a child’s feelings and preferences, these communities gradually draw children into the shared work and rhythms of daily life.

As well, Nikhil Chaudhary and Annie Swanepoel (2023) suggest that hunter‑gatherer‑like caregiving practices likely protect child mental health, implying that modern deviations from these patterns may create vulnerability.

These ideas point us in the same direction: culture and family ecology may matter more for children’s emotional well-being than modern mental health discourse often acknowledges.

Contrasting Temper Tantrums in Indigenous and Western Cultures

As an example, compare how many Indigenous cultures and modern parents respond to temper tantrums.

Research and clinical experience both suggest that children—whether neurotypical or neurodivergent—often respond poorly when adults become highly engaged during a tantrum. Some parents lecture, reason, coax, or scold, while others follow social media advice and attempt to soothe or “co-regulate” their child. Attention can increase arousal rather than reduce it.

This is one reason Doucleff’s observations are so striking. She describes Inuit parents as remarkably calm and often relatively emotionally unreactive during children’s outbursts. When children cry, hit, or act out, these parents do not typically launch into lengthy explanations or urgent attempts to talk the child down. Instead, they remain composed and wait for the storm to pass. This approach also closely resembles what evidence-based treatments teach parents to do.

Modern parents are also increasingly told to “talk things out” with angry children as if every moment of dysregulation calls for a therapeutic discussion. Not every behavior requires a diplomatic summit.

In many traditional communities, a parent is also less likely to carry this burden alone. Child-rearing is distributed across a wider caregiving network of grandparents, aunts, uncles, siblings, and other adults. This matters because calm parenting is much easier when adults are not parenting in a state of chronic depletion.

Expectations of Contribution and Autonomy Across Cultures

Doucleff’s work also highlights another major difference between traditional communities and modern Western families: children in those communities are expected to contribute. Maya families, for example, are described as raising cooperative children without relying on bribery, chore charts, threats, or repeated reminders, in part by including children in household tasks from the time they can walk.

Modern families, by contrast, often devote tremendous time and energy to entertaining children, protecting them from frustration, and over-negotiating ordinary responsibilities.

Doucleff also argues that children in traditional cultures are often granted more genuine autonomy. They are allowed to observe, explore, and gradually master meaningful roles within the family, all while remaining connected to a larger social group. This kind of autonomy appears to build competence and confidence, whereas modern overinvolvement and adult micromanagement may undermine both (Gray, 2021).

Stressed, isolated, and overwhelmed adults who are urged to overmanage children’s emotions while undermanaging behavior can easily see problems snowball. Children who might have grown into competence with multigenerational support, contribution, and calm authority instead become more anxious, inattentive, demanding, oppositional, or emotionally volatile.

The Role of Diagnosis and Labels in Modern Childhood Mental Health

If these problems continue, parents often seek professional treatment for the child. Eventually, a child picks up a diagnosis—or several. That diagnosis then becomes part of the family story: the child has oppositional defiant disorder, ADHD, anxiety, pathological demand avoidance, and so on.

It is worth asking whether some of what is labeled as psychopathology might instead be a predictable response to how more sensitive children are being raised in the 21st century.

Doucleff’s work is useful here because it makes one point unmistakably clear: Many behaviors that modern Western parents and professionals now treat as disorders might be very different had they grown up in more traditional settings.

That does not prove that modern family structure explains every childhood mental health problem. Still, it strongly suggests that culture and family organization may play a larger role than contemporary mental health discourse often acknowledges.

What Contemporary Families Can Learn from the Past

None of this means modern families need to become hunter-gatherers to raise healthy children. Doucleff and others are not arguing that people should abandon modern life or romanticize the past.

The point is simpler and more practical: Children appear to do well when they are surrounded by calm adults, included in meaningful family life, expected to contribute, and guided with steady, loving authority rather than constant emotional management. Modern families can still move intentionally toward that kind of home.

Nor does it mean that mental health diagnoses are never valid or useful. ADHD is real, but currently, nearly one in five adolescent boys in the U.S. has been diagnosed with ADHD (CHADD, 2025). Shouldn’t we be asking ourselves whether what’s happening around these kids is playing a role rather than only considering what might be happening inside of them?

All of this seems deeply unfair to both children and their families. Kids deserve better than to be labeled as the problem and prescribed medications that sometimes only address behavior on the surface.

This is not only ineffective; it is unjust.

These children are not broken. In many cases, they are responding exactly as one would expect them to in families that are isolated, stretched too thin, disconnected, and following unhelpful parenting advice.

item.title: Finding Dr. Right: The First Step to Effective Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Finding Dr. Right: The First Step to Effective Therapy

Mutual evaluation in early therapy sessions sets the tone for healing work.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Finding the right therapist is a bit like dating. You might get lucky with the first one, but you may not.
  • Making a choice among several therapists is more likely to lead to a good match because you see options.
  • Comparing your responses to several therapists taps into your agency and helps you identify your values.

At some point in my sophomore year of college, I found myself crying. A lot. For no reason. I worried I might be having a nervous breakdown, which would mean the unthinkable—that I’d flunk out of the university I’d worked so hard to get into. Having no idea what to do, and no one I dared ask, I did something like Googling local psychiatrists and going to the first one listed.

With his fancy office and framed certificates, he was clearly legitimate. But he was also a balding middle-aged man who smoked nauseating cigars and no matter what crazy fears were pouring out of me, he kept telling me I was in love with him. No. I wasn’t. Still, it took me six months to quit. A year later, in desperation, I tried again with my housemate’s therapist and got lucky. He was a kind and jolly man who kept me together until I graduated.

By the time I decided to get to the bottom of my problems, I was in my late 20s and knew enough not to rely on dumb luck. Instead, I turned to a concept my mother drummed into me: in all things, comparative shop. She wouldn’t buy gloves before checking out three sales. I got it. Instead of giving into overwhelm, passivity, and confusion, look at several options to gauge the quality of each, the cost/benefit, and, which you’re most drawn to—whether it’s gloves or a brain surgeon.

Finally, that’s what I did to find a therapist and learned that having made a choice rather than just letting something happen was therapy in itself because it meant tapping into my own agency and figuring out what I wanted. That process led to a great analyst who got to the bottom of my problems and changed my life. But she didn’t just materialize. First, I read through Psychology Today’s “Find a Therapist” listings and telephoned five who seemed plausible. I asked outright if they had children, explaining why that was important to me. I told them why I wanted therapy and listened carefully to their responses. One spoke a bit too aggressively; another was too tentative. I made consultation appointments (they’re often free) with the three remaining “possibles” in person. Zoom works, too, but not for me. I brought questions. Were they responsive and talky or more reserved? I wanted the former. Did they work with dreams? I had a lot of them. As I listened to what they had to say, I learned what I valued: warmth, earthiness, confidence, engagement.

Once I chose, I never considered switching—despite her being more than a decade younger than me, from a very different cultural background, and with a frilly feminine style unlike my own. She was the guide who took me to places inside myself I’d never been.

Such is my patient perspective. But I recently found myself wondering what a therapist would say. Knowing as much as they do, how do they choose their therapists? Even more intriguing, how do they choose their patients? For the therapist perspective, I asked Amy Albert, LMFT, LPCC, an experienced Los Angeles therapist (soon to be analyst as well). Here’s what she said:

"Comparison shopping is a smart way to think about the search. There’s a lot of hesitation about acknowledging that’s what you’re doing, as if it’s impolite, rather than good self-advocacy.

Six years ago, in a fog of grief about the death of my therapist, I too went therapist shopping. The first person I talked to was kind but sounded distant. The second one as well. The third answered my questions with a plain-spokenness that won me over. He was at ease with himself, a quality I wanted more of for myself. In psychoanalysis, we call this an ego ideal; that feeling of ‘you’ve got something I want.’ I felt both mutual understanding and chemistry.”

And what’s going on for you when a new patient comes for a consultation? I asked Amy, assuming that the therapists must be assessing, too. They are, but not in the way I imagined, as Amy explained.

"So many feelings come up when I’m sitting with a new patient. Excitement, curiosity, hope. Admiration! Someone walking through my door with the trust to consider therapy—that’s deeply moving.

When a patient comes to check me out, I’m also checking myself out. I keep close tabs on what’s going on for me. Am I curious about you? Do I feel that I can come to understand you and help you?”

And how do you know? I asked.

"Curiosity is a good sign. When I say ‘tell me more,’ I mean it. I can’t recall a time when I didn’t feel curious about a new patient, but if I weren’t, it would probably mean that I’m not the right match. I’d be frank about that and offer referrals.”

What happens if a patient is shy, shut down, or silent?

“That does happen. Some people come to treatment expecting therapy to be done to them, when therapy is a collaboration. But for many people, talking can be hard, and I’m aware that saying everything is a really tall order, especially in the beginning. Silences exist to leave space for you to have as many thoughts and feelings as possible.

But a therapist’s silence can be misunderstood as a void that leaves the other person feeling as if I’m bored. Then I might ask them what’s it like being here? I’ve had patients tell me they don’t like the silence, and that’s a conversation I welcome, because when a patient asks for what they need, it moves the work forward.

Whatever happens, that first 50 minutes is for us both to see how we are together. Inevitably, we do.”

What strikes me in Amy’s words is how much both patient and therapist can learn about one another in those first encounters, and about themselves.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The View From the Far Side
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

The View From the Far Side

A historian of state violence who became a patient and a prisoner.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Anosognosia, the brain's inability to recognize its own illness, can leave the sufferer the last to know.
  • Medication can steady the brain's storms but, research suggests, cannot by itself rebuild a disrupted life.
  • Decades of research point to connection as a condition of recovery, not just a supplement to treatment.
Source: Rodion Lobanov/Pexels

The most dangerous thing about losing your mind is that, from the inside, it can feel like finally finding it.

In the autumn of 2024, I moved through the world with a certainty I had chased my whole intellectual life. I am a historian by training. The grievances I had accumulated against my family, against former colleagues, against a mental health system that had failed me for the better part of a decade all fit together with an elegance that felt, in the moment, not like madness but like clarity. I was not unraveling. I was, I believed, finally seeing.

In fact, I was in the grip of a manic psychotic episode that would end with felony charges, four months in a county jail, and commitment to a state forensic psychiatric hospital. The clarity was the illness. That is the first thing I want this column to take seriously: severe mental illness does not always announce itself as suffering. Sometimes it arrives wearing the face of insight, and the person living inside it is the last to know.

I am qualified to write about this in two ways that rarely occupy the same person.

The first is that I am a scholar. I hold a doctorate in history from the University of Chicago, and my first book was about state violence and the institutions societies build to contain it. I understood confinement as a subject.

The second is that I became its object. The institutions I had studied with a scholar's authority—the hospital, the jail, the apparatus of psychiatric power—I came to know as a prisoner without a name. I have been the patient given 15 minutes a month with a psychiatrist who never once asked me a personal question. I have been the man in a 4-by-4 cell, holding my face up to a thin draft from an air duct because it was the only thing in that room moving toward me rather than away. I have read my own medical records and found a stranger described there, in the flat language of risk.

This column is written from both of those vantages at once—the distant one I kept as a scholar, and the one I reached only from inside.

American psychiatry has become very good at one thing and oddly unable to do another. It can match a diagnosis to a medication. It can steady a storm in the brain, and this matters: once a doctor finally named my bipolar disorder, after years of treating the wrong one, lithium quieted storms in me that nothing else could touch, and I am grateful for it every day.

But medication, however necessary, cannot by itself rebuild a life. It cannot restore the relationships the illness dismantled. It cannot answer the question every seriously ill person is finally asking beneath the symptoms: is there anyone who will still try to see me?

That question is not in the diagnostic manual. There is no billing code for it. The system has quietly decided it is someone else's problem.

article continues after advertisement

This, I think, is the deepest error of the medical model as we now practice it: not that it treats the brain, but that it treats the brain as though it were the whole person. Kay Redfield Jamison puts it exactly in Fires in the Dark: "To treat, even to cure, is not always to heal."

What healed me, in the end, was not only the medication. It was a recreational therapist who fell into step beside me on my courtyard runs, not to monitor me but to keep me company. It was a psychologist who asked about my mother instead of my blood levels. It was my mother herself, who drove every week for 10 months to sit with me in rooms designed to discourage intimacy, and who decided, against considerable evidence, that the sick man sending cruel emails and the son she had raised were the same person, and that the son was still in there, worth waiting for.

None of that is reimbursable. All of it was essential. The science has a name for what was happening in those encounters—limbic resonance, the synchronizing of one nervous system with another. But you don't need the term. It is what it feels like to be known and seen. And the accumulating evidence, from the Surgeon General's warning that loneliness is a public health emergency to decades of outcomes research, points toward a conclusion psychiatry has been slow to absorb: connection is not a supplement to treatment. It is a condition of recovery.

That the system so rarely delivers this is not mainly the fault of the clinicians inside it, most of whom are running triage in a system built for security rather than care. We fund the locks and the liability; we have never funded the time that healing takes. The biopsychosocial model is not so much rejected as quietly unfunded.

So that is what Minds at War will examine, week by week. Why mania can feel like genius. Why a person can lose the very capacity to recognize that they are ill—a neurological condition called anosognosia—and what that does to the families shut out by laws meant to protect a patient from everyone but his own illness. Why the system answers danger but not suffering, so that care arrives only after the harm is done. What we lost in trading the talking cure for the prescription pad, and what we'll lose again trading the pad for an all-too-complimentary AI therapist in an app. And what real recovery—not symptom management, but the slow return to oneself and to others—actually asks of us.

article continues after advertisement

Some weeks I will write as a historian, some weeks as a patient, because the truth needs both. And I will try to be honest about the harm I caused as well as the harm done to me. Severe illness does not absolve, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Source: Alexey Chudin/Pexels

There is a quality of starlight I keep returning to. The light you see arriving from a distant star left its source years ago; you are always looking into the past when you look up to the night sky. What I could not see during the years I was ill, I can see now, from the only vantage that made the seeing possible: the far side of it. But unlike starlight, that kind of delayed seeing can do something. It can be written down. It can reach someone still standing in the dark.

That is why I'm here. I'm glad you are, too.

item.title: When a Good Friendship Turns Bad
item.description:
Friends

When a Good Friendship Turns Bad

4 indicators that a friendship has become toxic.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • A good friendship can turn bad.
  • 4 signs indicate that the friendship is is detrimental to your emotional well being.
  • Chasing a friend who emotionally mistreats you may dismantle your mental health.
  • You may need to quietly mourn the friendship and move on.

Good friends are hard to come by, so when you find someone in your adult life that you click with, it is fantastic. You share the same sense of humor, hobbies, palette, or just simply enjoy each other’s company because it is easy. It’s refreshing to have someone in your life that you do not have tension or conflict with… until you do. Hurt and confused, you try to bring the “weirdness” up, but your friend gets defensive, and things escalate. Now, things are worse than ever.

You are flooded with anxiety and self-doubt for days. You cannot sleep and you must force yourself to eat. At this juncture, it is critical to your mental health to know how you should proceed. Should you pursue your friend and fight for the friendship, or should you let this person go? Four indicators may help you decide.

Four Red Flags That You May Need to Reevaluate the Relationship

First, has the friend exhibited signs of jealousy? For example, are they surprised that you got the promotion or job that you have always wanted? They seem supportive, when you tell them, but they also appear slightly agitated and make a couple of critical comments like, “Don’t have another break down on your first day,” or “I hope your boss doesn’t care about the hundreds of sticky notes you use to stay on track. Most professionals use calendars these days.” Their usual good-natured tone is replaced by a snarky one that leaves you with a chill.

Also, they start “drama” the night before your big day. They send you a curt and cryptic text, out of the blue. You reply politely, wishing to avoid drama at a time when you must have your wits about you. At the end of your first day, you hope that you receive a celebratory text, as you have done for your friend on numerous occasions, but you don’t hear from them at all, and you are devastated.

Second, you get the funny feeling that they are talking about you behind your back. You see a couple of posts on social media with them and your mutual friends. Initially, you are hurt that they did not include you, but you recognize that you have been busy. Yet, more pictures follow, so you try to connect with a few of these friends, but they don’t respond. When you see them at an event, they dote over your friend but give you the cold shoulder. You wonder what your friend has been saying about you, but nobody will give you the time of day.

Third, they blindside you by popping up in your life when you least expect it. For example, they show up at your new job with a sweater that you left at their place a few weeks ago. Startled, but happy that they care, you rush to them for a hug, but they react coldly. They leave as quick as they arrived and, on their way out, you see them chatting with some of your new colleague’s. You worry that they are trying to sabotage your new job, but then feel completely paranoid. After they leave, your co-workers comment on how “lovely” they are. Your head spins and you feel nauseous. You wonder if you are going “crazy.”

article continues after advertisement

Fourth, they act like nothing has happened. They invite you to lunch and despite the anxiety this causes, you agree. They are cheerful and talkative, which is a little bonkers considering how much they have impacted you lately. During the lunch they talk about spending a lot of time with a close friend, and they brag about their new work project. You validate both their new friendship and their achievement. As the meal goes on, they fail to ask you about your new job or your latest accomplishments. Glibly, they instruct you to pay because they say they need to leave quickly to make it to a work event.

Why These Behaviors Signal Emotional Mistreatment

You are angry, hurt, and dumbfounded. What the heck happened to your friend and your friendship? ---- As difficult as it is, you may need to let this friend go because they exhibit four behaviors that are utilized by a person who emotionally mistreats others.

Feeling envious of a friend is human, but how a person handles their jealousy may be a problem. In the example above, the friend does not grapple with their jealousy constructively. They do not process it with you or a supportive person in their life to get empathy and relief. Instead, they act on it destructively by attempting to sabotage you by breaking down your mental health. They gaslight you, continually.

Next, they triangulate, meaning they talk about you behind your back to your mutual friends. Distorting things, they mischaracterize you and act like they are the victim. It is unreal to think that some adults do not consider another side to the story before condemning a friend, but unfortunately this is common. However, if you decide to seek out your mutual friends to tell them your side, they may be additionally rejecting because, to them, you are fueling the fight and continuing the drama. It can further estrange you from these friends. Alternatively, it may be best to take the high road and keep the issues with your friend between you and them, even though they did not do this.

article continues after advertisement

Then, the friend blindsides you by showing up unanticipated. This is a power play because they are not there to apologize or work things out, they want to unsteady you and gain more ammunition to misrepresent you. Due to their control issues, they also want to “spy” on you to see what you are up to. Essentially, they act aloof and cold, but they really want you to chase them, so they have the power. They bait you with a surprise visit.

What to Do When a Friend Exhibits These Red Flags

A friend who does these four things may be a person who does not handle their jealousy or insecurities constructively. It may be best to quietly mourn the loss of the friendship and move on without them. You can find more on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist; Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work and in Life.

item.title: Should You Go On Practice Dates?
item.description:
Mating

Should You Go On Practice Dates?

A practice date could make you more game in different ways.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • A practice date is going on a date with someone you're not that into just to sharpen your dating skills.
  • Practice dates can help lessen the butterflies associated with real dates with those who made your cut.
  • Your dating skills could be very rusty jf you have been very selective and haven't gone on many dates.
  • Practice dates themselves could lead to some surprising results because you may be more relaxed and open.
Practice may not make perfect. But in can make progress.
Source: Pew Nguyen from Pexels

In the TV series Ted Lasso, the titular character riffed off Allen Iverson's famous press conference rant when he fumed, "We're talking about practice. Not a game. Not the game. We're talking about practice." Lasso was actually trying to lasso his star player into understanding the importance of practice.

Well, when it comes to some social media influencers on TikTok and Instagram, they're talking about practice, too—in this case practice dates. Not a real date when you are already really into someone. Not "The Date" with someone in the running to be "The One." They're talking about going on dates with people whom you're not that into for the main purpose of getting dating practice. That's to sharpen your dating skills for the real dates that supposedly matter more. The question then is are you game for this practice of going out on dates simply for practice?

The Rationale Behind Practice Dates

Getting more practice could help you better overcome those butterflies that you face when you are really into someone. You know when you forget things like the ability speak and your name. Those butterflies can grow to the size of Butterball chickens when you've been rather selective and haven't gone out on many dates in a while.

Practice can also help you refine those dating skills that you don't use on a regular basis—especially those skills that you only employ at the I-don't-know-much-about-you-yet-besides-your-face-and-body-and-that-you-claim-that-you-don't-like-drama stage of dating. This includes the ability to small talk, flirt, dress in an I'm-too-sexy-for-my-cat manner, and plan dates. That's why those just re-entering the dating arena after years of being in a long-term relationship can look about as out of place as leg warmers would in a party today.

Moreover, not everyone is the same when it comes to such dating skills. While some might be natural schmoozers, others may need more practice. And good dating skills do not necessarily correlate with good relationships skills. Take, for example, a woman whom I dated and admitted that she's good at dating but bad at relationships. Yes, take her.

article continues after advertisement

Attunement to the Range of Dating (and Human) Behavior

This brings up another potential benefit of getting more practice dating. It can help you become more attuned to picking up different cues and flags, including the red, green, and beige ones. The more you go on different dates, the more you may see recurring behaviors like love bombing, boundary pushing, future faking, and the blame game and get used to detecting and dealing with them.

Then there's this hot take—dating more can demystify those whom you initially find hot, too. Dating enough people of all types makes you realize even more that superficial looks do not necessarily correlate very well with the things that may matter more for long-term relationships like matching personalities, kindness, intelligence, and core values. People can end up surprising you in different directions, and each given date can proceed completely differently from how you originally intended.

How To Go On Practice Dates

Dating, especially early on, can involve using skills that you normally would not necessarily use in other situations, including relationships.
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko from Pexels

Speaking of which, intent is really what separates a practice date from a "real" date. A practice date on the surface can be everything that a real date might be, except that the intent is to just get some practice. You've chosen to go on a date with someone whom you normally wouldn't have chosen because that person somehow didn't meet your screening criteria. Maybe that person didn't have the right appearance, background, or whatever was needed to make the cut and instead landed up on your practice squad.

article continues after advertisement

The key, though, to getting in good practice for anything—whether it is a sport, playing an instrument, singing a song, baking a fruitcake, giving a talk, or dating—is to simulate game time conditions as closely as possible. That means doing everything that you would normally do so that you can really practice your skills.

That also means practicing with people who are decent and not gigantic pieces-of-you-know-what. Again, the goal is to practice your dating skills and not your debate, fighting, or escape skills. So, the best practice dates are the ones who seem quite decent as people but for whatever reason just don't set your loins on fire.

What Might Happen on a Practice Date

When you do go on a practice date, you may get exactly what you are looking for—practice. We're talking about practice. Not a game. Not the game. And that's still good for all the aforementioned reasons.

However, a funny thing may happen when you are just "practicing." You may actually be more game to connecting with people. Your guard may be down. The pressure may be off since you are assuming that this person is not in the running for your heart. That could leave you more open to be yourself and open to more possibilities and seeing people in different lights.

Consider this example. Someone recently told me that when she first met her longtime significant other, she was turned off to him. Her lack of interest then granted her more of a I'm-gonna-talk-about-whatever-I-want attitude on the date. Several hours later after lots of free talking, she apparently started realizing that he was more intriguing than she originally thought and that they actually had a lot in common beneath the surface.

So, going on practice dates can actually be a way of loosening up you dating criteria in a good way. It could bring you into closer contact with people who may have never made it to your dating game day lineup otherwise. And maybe, just maybe, this could help you better lasso or be lassoed by the person who ultimately is the right fit for you.

item.title: Social intelligence Arises Between Minds
item.description:
Neuroscience

Social intelligence Arises Between Minds

Neuroscience and AI research reveal cooperation as a shared neural emergence.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Social interaction may be the "dark matter" of AI: not a feature to add but a substrate intelligence requires.
  • In socially interacting mice, neural activity splits into a shared subspace and an individual one.
  • Trained to interact, artificial agents spontaneously develop shared neural patterns much like those in mice.
  • Natural and artificial brains converge on the same cooperative strategies, hinting at a shared social grammar.

Here is something odd about the most powerful artificial minds ever built. They can translate between a hundred languages, predict protein structures, and beat grandmasters at chess. Yet not one of them has ever truly interacted with another mind. Not in the way a three-month-old infant does when she locks eyes with her mother, their neural rhythms falling into sync, a feedback loop of mutual recognition spinning up between two brains that, for a few seconds, function as one.

We have built solitary thinkers at an extraordinary scale. What we have not built, or barely attempted, is intelligence that emerges in between.

Social Interaction as the Dark Matter of AI

Three years ago, my colleague Samuele Bolotta and I published a perspective paper arguing that social interaction is the "dark matter" of AI. The metaphor was deliberate. In physics, dark matter is not some exotic footnote; it constitutes most of the universe's mass and shapes the structure of everything we can see. We argued that the social dimension plays an analogous role: not a feature to bolt onto an already intelligent system, but the missing substrate without which certain forms of intelligence simply cannot arise.

The argument rests on a straightforward observation. Human cognition did not evolve in isolation. Theory of mind, metacognition, language: these are not fully hardwired modules. They are shaped through social interaction during development. As Cecilia Heyes has compellingly argued, they are "cognitive gadgets" assembled from cultural learning, not evolutionary instincts. From birth, we use other minds as scaffolding for building our own. Yet mainstream AI proceeds as if intelligence were a property of the solitary agent, a Cartesian thinker alone in its digital room, optimizing reward functions against an environment that happens to contain other agents but treating them as furniture.

We proposed three axes for what we called Social Neuro-AI: biologically inspired cognitive architectures, temporal coordination grounded in dynamical systems theory, and social embodiment. The framework was a roadmap. What we did not anticipate was how rapidly the empirical evidence would arrive.

Key Discoveries in Two Body Neuroscience: Shared Neural Subspaces

In 2025, two landmark papers, published simultaneously in Nature and Science, have brought the neuroscience of social interaction into direct dialogue with artificial intelligence.

Weizhe Hong's group at UCLA tackled a question that sits at the heart of what I have called "two-body neuroscience": what happens in the neural space between interacting brains? Using calcium imaging to record from molecularly defined neurons in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex of socially interacting mice, they discovered something elegant. The high-dimensional neural activity within each animal's brain can be decomposed into two distinct subspaces: a shared subspace, capturing shared dynamics across both animals, and a unique subspace, encoding what is specific to each individual.

article continues after advertisement

The surprise was in the cell types. GABAergic inhibitory neurons, a minority population in the cortex, contained a considerably larger shared neural subspace than excitatory glutamatergic neurons. The inhibitory architecture, it turns out, is disproportionately tuned to the social dimension. Notice that this shared subspace was not merely a byproduct of perceiving the same stimuli. It arose from the behaviours of both self and other, and it required direct, ongoing interaction to emerge.

Here is where it gets provocative. Hong and colleagues then trained reinforcement learning agents in a multi-agent environment and found that, as social interactions emerged, shared neural activity patterns also emerged between the artificial agents' networks. The patterns bore remarkable structural similarity to those observed in the mice. When they selectively disrupted the neural components sustaining these shared patterns, the agents' social behaviours collapsed. The shared subspace was not epiphenomenal. It was functional.

How Cooperation Emerges in Biological and Artificial Systems

Their companion paper in Science pushed the question further. Can we observe the emergence of mechanisms of cooperation in both biological and artificial systems? Jiang and colleagues designed an operant task requiring two mice to coordinate their nose-pokes within a narrow time window to receive mutual rewards. Through a series of elegant controls (opaque barriers blocking visual information, unilateral reward conditions), they demonstrated that success required genuine active coordination, not mere mimicry or coincidental timing.

The mice developed sophisticated strategies: approaching the action zone, waiting for the partner, holding back when the partner was absent, proceeding when coordination was possible. Neural recordings in the anterior cingulate cortex revealed that these decision processes — hold versus proceed, self-action versus partner-action — were explicitly represented in distinct neural populations. In the vocabulary of dynamical systems, the dyad had settled into a stable attractor that neither animal could have reached alone.

Then came the artificial parallel. Reinforcement learning agents trained on an analogous task independently developed convergent behavioural strategies and neural representations. Specific subpopulations within the artificial networks encoded cooperation-relevant decisions in ways that mirrored the biological brain. Targeted perturbation of these subpopulations disrupted coordination, revealing functionally distinct roles.

article continues after advertisement

The implication is clear: the computational architecture of cooperation may not be species-specific, or even substrate-specific. It may be a convergent solution, a kind of universal grammar of coordination, that any sufficiently complex system discovers when the task demands genuine joint action.

Studying AI As We Study Animals: A Neuroethological Approach

This convergence between biological and artificial systems is not a coincidence. It reflects a deeper methodological insight. A recent preprint from Kanaka Rajan's group at Harvard argues that deep reinforcement learning agents need to be studied the way neuroscientists study animals: with the tools of neuroethology (the study of neural systems in naturalistic behavioural contexts), not just reward curves. Using a complex foraging environment, Simmons-Edler and colleagues demonstrated that model-free agents can exhibit structured, planning-like behaviour through emergent activity alone, without explicit memory modules or world models. The key was looking beyond aggregate performance to analyze the joint structure of behaviour and neural representations.

This is exactly the kind of bridging that Social Neuro-AI demands. If we want to understand how social intelligence emerges in artificial systems, we need the same rigour we bring to studying it in biological ones. Beyond the technical challenge, there is a conceptual one: we lack the equivalent of ethograms for multi-agent AI, systematic catalogues of social behaviour that would let us compare artificial sociality with its biological counterparts.

The Question We Are Not Asking in AI

These papers collectively point toward a thesis that is both scientifically fertile and philosophically unsettling. Intelligence may not be a property that individuals possess. It may be a property that emerges between them. The shared neural subspaces Hong discovered are not confined to a single brain. They exist in the relational space between two. The cooperative strategies Jiang's mice invented were not individual solutions. They were dyadic achievements, irreducible to either animal alone. The neurobiologist Francisco Varela had a word for this: enaction, the idea that cognition is not representation of a pregiven world but the bringing forth of a world through interaction.

article continues after advertisement

If this is true for mice and for artificial agents trained with simple reward signals, what does it mean for the systems we are currently building at scale? Large language models are trained on the products of human social interaction (text, dialogue, arguments), but they have never participated in such interactions. They have consumed the residue of inter-brain coupling without ever coupling. They are, in a sense, raised on books about swimming without ever touching water.

The field of AI stands at a crossroads it has not yet fully recognized. We can continue building ever-larger solitary minds and hope that social intelligence emerges as a byproduct of scale. Or we can take seriously what neuroscience is telling us: that interaction is not a feature of intelligence but a constitutive condition for it.

The dark matter is not optional. It is what holds the galaxy together.

item.title: Psychotic Personality Organization and Defenses
item.description:
Psychosis

Psychotic Personality Organization and Defenses

Dissolution anxiety, primitive defenses, and the struggle for self-boundaries.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Most people organized at the psychotic level are not overtly psychotic.
  • The psychotic level of personality organization is characterized by fears of annihilation and engulfment.
  • The self-identity is too porous - the boundaries between the self and the universe are too blurred.
Source: The Scream - Edvard Munch, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

See below for more on this series of posts.

The three levels of personality organization in patient populations are neurotic, borderline, and psychotic.

Not everyone who is organized at the psychotic level is psychotic; in fact, most are not. Many people might appear fairly typical to others, but struggle with confusion about what is real or imaginary, or how separate or connected they are to the universe (4). All those who experience psychosis have at least for that period of time either regressed into the psychotic level or are typically organized at the psychotic level. In other words, to be overtly psychotic is to also be organized at the psychotic level of personality organization (necessary), but to be psychotically organized is not necessarily to be psychotic (not sufficient) (1, 4).

Clinical Features of the Psychotic Level of Organization

Please see this piece for the origins of the psychotic level of organization. The greatest fear of individuals organized at the psychotic level is dissolution; the disintegration of their already poorly bounded self into the universe. Analysts call it “annihilation anxiety”, and it is the anxiety that psychotic symptoms are designed to defend most vigorously against (5). From this perspective, these symptoms are not evidence of a mind in random disarray but organized primitive defenses against an unbearable anxiety. The fear is so visceral and existential that people have been known to faint or fully dissociate in the face of it. As Winnicott says in his paper Fear of Breakdown, on the nature of psychotic anxiety:

“I contend that clinical fear of breakdown is the fear of a breakdown that has already been experienced. It is a fear of the original agony which caused the defense organization which the patient displays as an illness syndrome” (6).

This feared fragmentation or dissolution is analogous to their experience of maternal engulfment, part of the origins of the psychotic organization. A mother who cannot allow for separation tends to unconsciously try to pull the child back into herself, like an amoeba surrounds its food source and envelops it for nourishment. Relatedly, the individual’s greatest wish is to be a fully separate, boundaried self, no longer at risk for splintering off into the universe or being swallowed whole by the mother.

The primary defenses that someone at the psychotic level uses to protect themselves from annihilation anxiety include withdrawal (”autistic withdrawal”), projection, projective identification, and denial (1, 2, 4). In projective identification, disowned parts of the self are unconsciously projected onto another person, who is then pressured, through the relationship itself, to think, feel, and act in accordance with the projection. In denial at this level, the individual does not merely minimize or avoid an uncomfortable reality, but rather entire aspects of internal or external experience are refused recognition, as though they simply do not exist. In autistic withdrawal, the individual turns inwards, into their own minds, losing themselves in intellectual ideas, fantasy, or sometimes delusion. The inward turn behaves like heavy walls around a castle – they are impregnable to encroachment by “enemy”, which in this case is the outside world that has brought the terrible fear of annihilation upon the person. The fantasies and delusions often mirror some of the dynamic conflicts and fears/wishes that led to the psychotic organization. Common themes include:

1. Being intruded on or penetrated, or other issues around absent or porous boundaries between the self and the world:

· ideas of reference,

· mind-reading

· being followed or persecuted

· belief that something has been inserted into the body

· alien abduction and penetration

2. Being one (aka unbounded) with the universe:

· strange connections between the person and their environment

· being all powerful

· a universal consciousness or Buddhist awakening

· being Jesus or God, or omnipotent or omniscient

· being supremely wealthy or in societal positions of power

· Being immortal

3. Beliefs around non-existence:

· The body is empty

· The body is missing organs or parts of organs

· the person is already dead, or inanimate like a robot

For some, it is easier to succumb to the seduction of their inner life where they can fully indulge in fantasies of all-powerful oneness with the universe. Others may be either more motivated to stay at least somewhat present in the real world, or take medications which make full retreat more difficult. For them, there is often a tension between the pull of fantasy and the hard work of staying present in our shared reality.

Anger at the psychotic level of organization includes strong projections of hostile, violent, or homicidal fantasies onto others. The anger can be frightening, explosive, and sometimes violent, as it manifests in sadomasochistic omnipotent fantasies of control (7). For those overtly psychotic, the completeness of the projection acts as a protection; the violent fantasy has been so thoroughly externalized that the person experiences themselves as the target of violence rather than its potential perpetrator.

But for those organized at the psychotic level without overt psychosis, the sadistic fantasy is not fully projected and remains ego-syntonic (experienced as a natural part of the self rather than as a symptom), and familiar or even pleasurable. When narcissistic grandiosity reinforces the conviction that such impulses are justified, or when antisocial traits remove the inhibitory weight of guilt and empathy, the sadistic fantasy can be enacted. It is at this point, when the fantasy is neither fully projected outward nor fully restrained internally, that the risk of violence is greatest.

In therapy, the original goals are more concrete than those at the neurotic or even borderline level of organization. The complexities of psychodynamic treatment at this level of organization warrant their own discussion. See here for how to start dynamic therapy for psychosis. In the early stages, the goal is to help the patient to see the therapist as a real person, and not as a hostile or idealized projection (1, 8). This may mean being more natural and even self-disclosing than one would be for a patient at a higher level of organization. Other early goals include helping the patient to identify their own thoughts, emotions, and even bodily sensations, as they often avoid mentalizing or consciously experiencing their feelings or body. Later the work is to help the patient experience these thoughts and feelings as belonging to their self in an effort to reaffirm the patient’s boundaried existence.

A non-psychotic patient organized at the psychotic level with obsessive-compulsive character traits:

He will present very differently than his overtly psychotic counterpart and may seem quite healthy on casual acquaintance. He experiences his obsessions and compulsions as ego-syntonic and beset by magical thinking, but is well skilled at masking his more bizarre ideas. He will “go down the rabbit hole” fairly frequently and get intensely embroiled in conspiracy theories. These become a holding place for his magical thinking and rigid obsessiveness and for a while it is all he thinks or wants to talk about, until he moves onto the next bizarre preoccupation. He is married to a woman who shares some of his strange beliefs, and they amplify and validate each other. At work he mostly knows to keep his magical thinking to himself, though he confides in a few colleagues that “most people don’t know the truth”, or “they’ve all swallowed the blue pill”.

He is unlikely to go to therapy without some provoking event. Like at the borderline level, he experiences the problems in his life as having an external cause. He will perhaps be convinced to come to therapy because of worsening panic attacks – in his case small moments of annihilation anxiety. Or he seeks help because his compulsions start to occupy too many hours of the day.

But he will be on his best behavior – guarding against the therapist learning about his strange views on life, in part because he worries that she cannot be fully trusted. Over time, she might begin to suspect that this well-groomed, polite, tightly wound man who she assumed was organized at a neurotic level might be more primitively organized, as she begins to learn his anxiety has a markedly paranoid flavor, and as the transference quickly becomes beset with projective identifications. These patients sometimes surprise therapists by developing a “psychotic transference”. The therapist did not realize that the patient was psychotically organized all along.

Two notes: I talk a lot about mothers. It is short-hand for “primary infant caregiver”, who is not always the mother.

This is the third of the three-part series (part 1) (part 2) on analytic approaches to personality organization and how we can use this framework to develop a psychoanalytic formulation of our patients.

item.title: AI and the Empowerment Paradox
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Empowerment Paradox

Can AI undermine the capacities that make human empowerment possible?

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • AI can expand what we do without developing who we are.
  • Effort once built capability, but now, convenience bypasses that process.
  • As AI grows more capable, our human role in our own development deserves a harder look.
Source: Image by Igor Link from Pixabay.

Every generation has had its version of this argument. The Greeks worried that the written word would weaken memory and produce the illusion of knowledge rather than knowledge itself. Calculators would hollow out mathematical intuition. Google would end the need to remember anything. We were mostly wrong each time, and the technologies mostly served us well.

But there's something different about this moment. AI doesn't just retrieve or calculate, it reasons and synthesizes. It operates in the cognitive space where we used to have to show up ourselves. And unlike the calculator, which still required you to understand what you were calculating, AI can produce a finished answer from a half-formed thought.

When Effort was the Point

I'll argue that capability and struggle were inexorably connected. You became a better writer by writing, sometimes badly, for years. You developed judgment by making decisions and then living with the consequences. The process was slow and often humbling, but the work changed the worker. That's not romantic nostalgia, it's a description of how human beings actually develop.

AI changes the equation. A difficult problem can be solved before you've had a chance to do your own work. Now, I'm not arguing that this is alway bad—at times it can be liberating, The same way elevators freed us from climbing stairs, or washing machines gave back hours we'd spent in drudgery. But there's a difference here that's critical. Elevators didn't atrophy our capacity for thought, but AI might.

What Empowerment Actually Demands

Think about this, empowerment has never been just about outcomes. A student who receives a correct answer may get the A, but not much more. A person who outsources those difficult decision hasn't developed judgment. They've borrowed it. And borrowed judgment, like borrowed certainty, can't really stand up to life's difficult situations.

This is the paradox that interests me. It's about technology powerful enough to expand human capability that may simultaneously make the pursuit of that capability feel unnecessary. It's not built on malice, but delivered with convenience. The friction that once built something in us begins to disappear. And we might not notice that until it's too late.

The Bigger Question

I'm not worried about AI becoming more intelligent. It will, at least from a computational perspective. What I'm more interested in is what human participation starts to look like as this happens. I'm interested in whether we remain genuinely engaged with our own thinking or if we start treating our own cognition as a less capable or efficient option.

article continues after advertisement

Empowerment has always been something you do—not simply a result or outcome. In essence, it's a roadmap to being. Education empowers because it transforms the person learning. Relationships empower because they require actual investment. Experience empowers us because it leaves a path. In each case the value isn't just the result but the process of our discovery and formation.

AI doesn't automatically threaten any of that. But it does, for the first time, make the shortcut almost indistinguishable from the work. And that is an essential insight. The danger isn't that AI reduces human capability. In many ways it expands it dramatically. The essential and deeper question is whether capability alone is enough. If empowerment depends on the development of a constellation of human capabilities that include judgment, resilience, creativity, and agency, then a technology can increase what we are able to do while reducing our participation in becoming the kind of people who can do it.

This is the empowerment paradox. The more capable AI becomes, the more important it is to ask what role remains for the human beings using it.

item.title: Helping Kids Feel They Matter
item.description:
Parenting

Helping Kids Feel They Matter

Contributions at home and in the community support thriving.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Mattering means children feel seen, heard, and valued, building resilience and self-worth.
  • Kids who feel they matter are less likely to engage in risky behaviors and have better wellbeing.
  • Starting early with small tasks and volunteering builds a child’s sense of significance.
  • Kids who feel they matter can ward off teasing and bullying more easily.
Source: Alina Rossoshanka / Pexels

We all know that mattering is important. But what is it exactly? And how can we help our children to feel they matter?

Mattering is the sense of feeling valued (Cornwall, 2023). Children who feel they matter feel seen, heard, and important. This feeling is vital to their sense of personal significance, connectedness, and social acceptance, as well as being an important source of resilience and adaptability (Flett, et al, 2021 ).

When a child feels they matter, this forms a protective shield against the teasing and other forms of mistreatment that inevitably occur in childhood (Flett et al, 2021). In fact, developing a sense of mattering can also reduce negative feelings about the self as well as reducing or inhibiting the development of suicidal feelings and ideas (Flett et al) and other problematic behaviors.

Teenagers who feel like they matter to their families are less likely to binge drink and struggle with addiction, and they are more likely to experience happiness, self-compassion, empathy, self-efficacy, resilience, academic achievement and life satisfaction.

Helping Kids Feel That They Matter

A sense of mattering can come from various sources. Of course, the child must feel loved by those important to him or her, and they must be treated like they matter - both at home and at school. But they also must have real opportunities to make a contribution. Ideally, this should happen at home, at school and in the larger community.

Parents who are already overwhelmed with all the responsibilities of work and parenthood may wonder how they are going to do this on top of everything else they do!

But this is important.

Concrete Strategies to Introduce At All Ages

- Start early.

- Young children can begin to help around the house. They can do very simple jobs and you can tell them how proud you are of them when they finish. Even if they refuse at first, keep encouraging them. Make screen time contingent on doing certain tasks - or allow them to earn screen time by doing these tasks.

- Children as young as four or five can join in on community activities such as street clean-ups, collecting clothes and taking them to Goodwill or donating food for those in need. Make sure you explain what they are doing and why it is important.

- Older children can join you in doing a few hours of volunteer work each week. You can do this through your place of worship or local community organizations. And again, talk about why it is important for them do this and why you like to spend time doing this. Emphasize their importance to others when they do this.

- Try to find volunteer opportunities for your teens in the community. Fire or ambulance stations often have first aid, choke-saving and babysitting courses. And sometimes there are opportunities for teens to actually work there as helpers or junior EMTs. Nursing homes and continuing care facilities often allow teens to volunteer as do some hospitals. Find something that could be interesting to your teen and encourage them to take part. Do some hours with them if that will help them to go. And in the end, after helping your child to get involved and after getting involved yourself, you may find that you feel you matter more than you thought as well!
